utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. 1531, independently of the fact that you say that you know nothing about Cengic's interview, the one that I quoted, tell me, please, what was the first knowledge you had about the arming of Muslim forces in Foca? Since what he says here, that from the 1st of August there were forces which possessed automatic rifles, machine-guns, mortars, and so on, the 1st of August, 1990, in fact he quotes, six months prior to the formation of the Patriotic League itself. So please tell me what you know about arming.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question yesterday, and all I can say is that I really knew nothing about arming at that time, nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday when you told me that you had read the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when did you learn of any Muslim arming at all? When was the first time you learnt about that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never learnt anything in concrete terms in view of the fact of what I said yesterday in private session when I explained the specific features of my role.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know that after these events that took place in Foca, the ones you're testifying about, Halid Cengic went to Visoko where he was one of the main initiators of the exodus of the Serb population in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just said I was not aware of it, but I did learn through the information media, the writings in the press, that he assumed an important position in the Bosnia-Herzegovina army in that small town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know precisely what kind of ethnic cleansing was conducted in that small town as you call it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I remind the accused that we're presently in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry, Ms. Pack. I won't say anything that would point to this witness's identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statements, Witness, you depict the following picture, if I understand it correctly: You say that the Serbs were arming themselves and preparing for war, whereas the Muslims were not arming themselves or, rather, that you knew nothing about any kind of preparation for arming, even after the large rally that took place, rallying over 100.000 people as you yourself said, in Foca, and the SDA activities along those lines. Is that right, Mr. 1531?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I told you what I knew, and I can't tell you what I don't know about and haven't got any arguments to put forward on something that I have not been kept abreast of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I'm not going to go into the details of your statement because I really don't know what all the things that could have been going on there, but I would like to focus on certain portions where you say some things which quite simply I'm just not able to understand, and I would even say they sound rather ridiculous and even grotesque. For example, in the last paragraph on page 2 of your statement of the 25th of June, 1996, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted); then we have Petko Cancar and Miro Stanic. So the president of the Serbian Democratic Party in Foca who, by the by -- who, by the way, were being seen together. They came to Foca together from Sarajevo. And generally speaking, they were public personages, representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, in fact. Now, they were having a meeting, as you say, in a church in Foca. Tell me now, please, Mr. 1531, isn't this - how shall I put this? - a ridiculous assertion that personages of that rank could meet anywhere they like, and they were seen publicly around town, they all had public offices, now suddenly they have to organise some clandestine meetings in a church in Cerezluk, and just the two of them who would usually be seen around town in public. Isn't that nonsense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If, 1531, you wish to go into private session to answer that question, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you please look at paragraph 5 of your statement. It is marked with the number 5. It is page 3 of the B/C/S version. The first paragraph. Page 3, first paragraph of the B/C/S, paragraph 5. It's at the top of that page. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: This is, I assume, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which statement? Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which date, please, so we can get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25th of June, tab 3, received from the OTP. Tab 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to give a more detailed answer to this question, I would ask Their Honours to allow for a private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will not ask anything that could reveal his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he's worried about it, though, he can go into private session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that same statement --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In that same statement, look at paragraph 15, please, in which you talk about the armed attack on Foca. And you say that a Serb woman was wounded. Would you explain to Their Honours, please, who carried out that attack and how that Serb woman was wounded on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that fire from Serbian paramilitary forces were opened on the 8th of April, and that is when that woman was wounded close to the KP Dom, the prison. And this place is known as the Ivanovici houses, that is, the houses of the Ivanovic family, and sniper fire was opened from there. The telephone lines were working, and it was reported by people who have houses nearby, as well as companies, that the woman had been hit. They knew the woman, and I was called up by the president. I think -- I think we have to go back into private session if I have to elaborate on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to do that unless you want particularly, Mr. Tapuskovic, any more detail about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Since I have to economise with the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 29 again, please. You say -- you talk first about Serb paramilitary units that were directing artillery and machine-gun fire. I think this is in the fourth sentence. And then later on you say: "There was some resistance in those parts of town, but it was sporadic and of a limited nature." Could you explain what the resistance was like and who was putting up that resistance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I could hear from where I was, that is, sporadic shooting with infantry weapons as opposed to artillery fire towards those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you went on to say: "The Muslims who lived there had very little weapons, and later on all ethnically mixed parts of town were exposed to sniper fire." How do you explain that that fire lasted simultaneously towards the parts of town in -- with mixed populations, where both Serbs, Croats and Muslims lived? Was this some sort of a conflict that was going on there and then those involved in the conflict didn't pay any attention to where which civilians were living?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were sniper nests held by Serb paramilitary units, and in mixed environments, the situation was under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must apologise first. I must ask you, did you say that the area in which you lived, did Radivoj -- did Radovan Karadzic come there? Did you say that yesterday? I just want to check.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't mention Karadzic in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So he was never there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but here in paragraph 35 you said --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1531 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this paragraph, there is a description of the situation in Foca and that the orders came directly from Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go into private --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Go into private session to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1531, that concludes your evidence. Thank Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go. If you would just wait for the blinds to be lowered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Harland who is to be recalled. He is, I gather, ready to come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. While we're waiting for him, I've been asked to clarify the position of about an exhibit. It's the Pale speech which was marked for identification. I think it was Exhibit 569, tab 9. I will be told if I'm wrong. In any event, it's some days ago, and the registry want it clarified. I don't remember myself why it was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think this is the one that was produced in two parts. Mr. Groome can deal with it, and I think I mentioned it yesterday, it's now in a comprehensive format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you recall the testimony of Mr. Donia, the Prosecution marked for identification the entire Assembly minutes but just introduced excerpts. During the course of the cross-examination, the Chamber indicated that it would be helpful to have the entire -- entirety of this session translated and introduced into evidence, and that is what we provided the Chamber on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. So this is -- the exhibit is no longer marked for identification, Exhibit 538 tab 9; it becomes an exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I assume the usher is collecting the witness. When she's brought him in, I'll get her to put the Sarajevo map back in the position it was if it's thought helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, if you'd like to take a seat. You, of course, remain under the declaration which you took on the last occasion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will I have a set of the documents that were submitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you should have the documents. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You've got just over two and a half hours left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, since your testimony was interrupted, I have to say in advance or, rather, I would like to make a reservation in advance. I'm not quite sure that the notes that I took during the examination-in-chief always referred to what you yourself were saying. Perhaps they refer to another witness. So please, would you tell me if I make some mistakes, because it's very difficult when testimony is heard in two parts for me to find my way in my notes and documents. So please would you bear that in mind, because I won't intentionally be asking you questions which you didn't refer to and didn't testify about. Quite simply, it might just be a mistake on my part because of the interruption that has occurred, the two-part testimony. We started by looking at the map and the comments made with regard to this Sarajevo map, and most of your testimony referred to Sarajevo, in fact. So it would be a good idea, since you spent a long time in Sarajevo yourself, you had many contacts with people, you knew everything about the Serb positions and the Muslim positions, so it would be a good idea if you were to compare that map and what you knew about the deployment of forces in Sarajevo with this map that I have here. It is a map of Sarajevo showing -- and it says, it's in English, "Ethnic map of Sarajevo on the basis of the population census of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of the 31st of March, 1981." That's the title of the map itself. And you can see on it what the ethnic make-up of Sarajevo looked like at that time. And my question is very short one. It is this: Roughly, or to what extent, to the best of your knowledge, does the deployment of Serb and Muslim positions coincide with this map? I assume the question is clear. Please go ahead. And all the explanations are given in English on the map, the text isn't long, so I'm sure you'll be able to find your way around it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have the map placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. The map of ethnic distribution only very partially reflects the final confrontation lines. In general, certainly the Serbs secured the areas around Sarajevo, the less densely inhabited areas in which they had been a majority. Many of the mixed areas, mixed, predominantly Muslim and Serb but also with some Croat areas, in the urban part of Sarajevo were secured by the -- by the Serbs at the beginning of the war. So, for example, though of course it's ten years ago so you will excuse me if I don't have the exact figures, I recall that Ilidza, in the urban area, the large part in the west, the urban area of Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you would point out on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area here. The Serb -- Serb forces secured that area and removed the Muslim population or it fled despite the fact that that area had a similar number of Muslims and Serbs immediately prior to the war, and in fact, I think, even a slight -- slightly larger number of Muslims. The same, I think, is true of some of the areas immediately north of the city. Vogosca and Ilijas, these areas were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could point on the ELMO so we can see on the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If you can't see what the regions indicate, you have a number on each municipality, to designate each municipality, and then you have the names of those municipalities. The Serb territories are blue; the lighter blue areas where the -- where the relative majority is, the darker regions the absolute majority, and the Muslim areas are green and yellow.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, this map -- and it doesn't mark who controlled which territory, it marks which population was the greater in 1981. It also doesn't have the names, it just has a series of numbers for most of the areas. Just a second. It's actually much easier for me to work off the big map, if nobody objects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Do that. It will be much easier for everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So prior to the war, the Muslims were a large majority in the municipality of Stari Grad, and that was held by the Muslims during the war. Almost all of the other downtown municipalities, that is Centar, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, and Ilidza were -- were heavily mixed, roughly equal in terms of their Muslim and Serb populations. And this area, of course, became divided by the confrontation line. The confrontation line came around here, around the municipality of Stari Grad, which was entirely held by the Muslims, and then the Grbavica section of Novo Sarajevo was held by the Serbs more or less down to the Miljacka river, cutting right through some of the buildings here on what I think is Ljubljanska Street. And then up here again the Muslims controlled these settlements. The Serbs controlled a part of Dobrinja. The Serbs controlled the airport at the beginning the war, and then, by agreement, allowed UNPROFOR to use it. And in the surrounding areas, which were mountainous areas, the Serbs in general were much more numerous than Muslims prior to the war, and those areas were held by the Serbs throughout the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you try again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, looking at this map which shows where the Serbs live and the Muslims live, because this is just a map of Sarajevo, can we say that mostly the forces deployed during the war were distributed in conformity with the territories on which each of the parties lived, more or less? Of course, it is impossible to have this coincide exactly, but predominantly so, that each side held its territory?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, that would not be true, because particularly in Sarajevo, particularly in the urban area, the populations were entirely mixed. And in a way, the larger ethnic map only gives you a sense of who is in which area, but of course the overwhelming bulk of the people actually lived in the urban area of Sarajevo, and that area was almost randomly mixed. Not entirely randomly; Stari Grad had a much larger Muslim population, some of the Stup settlement had a larger Croat population, but in general the urban population was mixed. And where -- where Serb forces took control of that, parts of that territory during the war, they did remove or kill or force to flee almost the entire non-Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. On this map, could you point out what the Serbs had occupied, what territory they had occupied where they did not live? The one on the overhead projector, what is it that they took control of and where they didn't themselves live, the areas not populated by them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I must say I don't like working from this map, because first of all it doesn't show the city of Sarajevo, it only shows ethnic groups, and it largely only has -- it has only numbers representing the geographical locations. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, let's deal with it this way: Since you're a witness in a court --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- and of course you must be accurate, if you feel that you cannot do justice on that map, then you should say so. If you can, of course, if you can answer, well, so much the better, but if you feel that it really isn't possible properly to answer, then I think you should revert to your other map. It's up to you how you feel about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is that the names of the cities appear on the -- over the page. Rear side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. That makes it particularly difficult to deal with it when it's on an overhead projector. Why don't I just refer to the large map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever you feel more comfortable with. If you can mention particular areas by name, then it might be easier, particularly any areas which the Serbs took over where they weren't a majority or something of that sort before, the areas you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. The built-up areas of Ilidza, of Novo Sarajevo, Grbavica settlement, of Vogosca, and just off the map, Ilijas, would have been areas where the population would have been mixed prior to the war, that is that no one population of the three ethnic groups, main ethnic groups of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would have had more than a third of the population, or would have had more than half of the population, anyway. And in those areas which were taken over by the Serbs which did not previously have a Serb majority, the -- the Serbs would have removed or caused to flee the non-Serb population. So I would mention Ilidza, Novo Sarajevo, Vogosca, and Ilijas in that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if we were to place this map over Sarajevo and the distribution of force if it were in the right ratio, do you have an idea of what percentage would not coincide with respect to the territory that belonged to them, and would there be a percentage that would be different regardless of movements up and down?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In geographical size, I couldn't tell you very exactly, but approximately -- approximately 100.000 non-Serbs, Muslims, Croats. Mainly Muslim but also Croats and people of mixed marriage found -- Sarajevans, found themselves in territories that by May of 1992 were controlled by Serb forces, and those people, some were killed but a larger number either fled to the Muslim-controlled part of Sarajevo or, in some cases, were able to flee the country altogether. So I would say the area of overlap, as you call it, would be an area affecting about 100.000 people of the total Sarajevo population of 400.000 or 500.000 people. So there was some overlap, yes. You are correct when you say there was some overlap between the Serb-held areas and the areas previously inhabited by Serbs. And similarly between Muslim-held territory and the territories previously inhabited by Muslims. But territory on which lived about a hundred thousand people would not be in that general statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the 150 Serbs from Sarajevo? 150.000 Serbs, I'm sorry? What about the 150.000 Serbs from Sarajevo? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, as you point out, many of them -- the great -- a majority of them were in territory which was immediately taken by Serb forces. So they were, as it were, within their -- the territory controlled by armed forces friendly to them. For the -- for the remaining Serb population, by the time I arrived in Sarajevo, which was in late May of 1993, we estimated that approximately 40.000 Serbs remained within the confrontation line, that is within the area controlled by the Muslim forces. Many of those people reported that their relatives had either fled at the beginning of the fighting or -- and many of those who remained did wish to leave the city but were not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they weren't able to. They weren't allowed to leave town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs did allow the Muslims to leave part of town which they held under their control, whereas the Muslims did not allow this to take place with respect to these 40.000 Serbs. They didn't allow them to leave the part of town they were in. Isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first part of your statement I wouldn't characterise like that, when you say the Serbs did allow the Muslims to leave. In fact, in most cases, they initially forced them to leave. But the second half of your statement I would have to acknowledge is correct, that many of the Serbs who were caught in the fighting and caught on the Muslim side of the confrontation line wished to leave and were not allowed to do so by the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you were an international official, I assume you know that it is the -- that the authorities must -- it is their duty to allow the population to leave a territory where a conflict is being conducted, and that that is a serious violation of the law if they keep the population back, the civilian population back in areas where conflicts are going on, this is a serious violation of the law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the positions you held, the United Nations in Sarajevo, did you take any steps to enable the population to take refuge and leave the area of conflict, to allow them to leave the area, those of them who wished to leave, and to go to where they wished to go?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I should say that from our perspective, it was not that we wanted freedom of movement for Serbs or for Muslims, but just we wanted -- we believed that freedom of movement for the civilian population at large was something which we should advocate for. And when I say that many of the Serbs, because we were talking about Serbs, in Sarajevo wished to leave, the Serb civilian population living in the Muslim-controlled area, I should also say that many of the Muslims and Croats and people of mixed nationality also wished to leave but were unable to. That doesn't change the general correctness of your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. statement, but it's worth clarifying. Now, we did take a number of measures. First, we -- we sought to tell all sides about their obligations under international law towards the civilian population, and we also sought to negotiate what we called Blue Routes, that is routes from Sarajevo to the outside world where both parties, both the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Muslims, and the Serbs would agree to allow certain numbers of civilians, usually, unfortunately, on a basis of a sort of ethnic equation they would make up between them, to allow them to leave the -- leave the city. And these so-called Blue Routes were open at various times. We also made provision so that people who were what we called humanitarian cases, people who were either very sick or who had been wounded, could in some cases be evacuated by us from the airport which we controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Harland, do you know why the conflict broke out between Muslims and Croats at the beginning of your term in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly heard the views at great length of the leaders of both the Muslim and the Croat communities, because that -- that conflict was just beginning on my arrival and was very much on the minds of both our Muslim interlocutors and our Croat interlocutors, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were there virtually throughout the time of the conflict between Muslims and Croats. It started when you arrived, and it went on for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was precisely during those conflicts that the Serbs made it possible to save many thousand Croats where they were threatened with destruction by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that was not true in my experience, except in some limited cases. It is true that we saw that the Serbs provided weapons to the Croat enclave of Kiseljak. The Serbs had a small access to the Croat enclave of Kiseljak I think at a village called Kobiljaca. And they provided weapons, including tanks, we were able to observe moving there. Also, after the Muslim forces took, captured the Croat enclave of Vares, it is true that the Serbs provided access through their territory to Croats fleeing by bus from that area. So, yes, I was aware of some assistance provided by the -- by the Serbs to the Croats during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For example, you mentioned only Vares. Let me not mention the others, but you could mention them. How many thousand Croats did the Serbs evacuate so that they wouldn't be the victims of the Mujahedin in those days? They made it possible for them to leave across their territories, to go where they wanted, to avoid certain destruction and extermination in those enclaves of theirs. Well, let's look at Vares alone. How many thousand Croats?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer recall the exact number of Croats evacuated from Vares. I -- to Kiseljak. I would believe it was probably in the region of 5.000. I should -- I should add, though, that the people -- the people who stayed -- and we had a lot of opportunity to observe this. The Croats who stayed in territory controlled by the -- by the Muslims, their treatment varied a lot. There were some, as in Tuzla, for example, who did not seem to experience negative treatment. When you said, you know, were they victims -- you know, that they were victims of the Muslims, that's -- there certainly were areas where Croats were expelled from their homes and their homes were burnt and some Croats were killed, and I myself saw some of that in -- after the fall of Kakanj with the activities of the 7th Muslim Brigade, but in most places that I visited where there were Croat communities living on Muslim-held territory, they were -- they were probably the object of discrimination, but they were not, in my experience, in physical danger except in a few cases. So it's actually not good to make a direct comparison between their condition, for example, and the condition of non-Serbs in Serb territory. In most of the places I visited in Serb-held territory, those who remained, the non-Serbs who remained, would have been in serious physical danger except in a few places, perhaps Banja Luka and Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Harland. So as not to waste any time, you're saying that only in a few places where Serbs were in control, the non-Serbs lived normally. Only in a few places, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And also, you're claiming that during the Muslim-Croat conflicts, the Croats lived normally in places held by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a mixed picture, but in some places they were able to continue with normal life and to some extent, like in Sarajevo and in Tuzla, as normal as the conditions of the war allowed. But in some places, particularly the smaller communities of Central Bosnia, there was ethnic cleansing by the Mujahedin or the 7th Muslim Brigade. I was able to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And according to the information available to you, how many Croats were killed in Central Bosnia and how many were ethnically cleansed by the Muslims from areas in which they had lived?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The numbers killed we believed to be relatively low compared to the casualties of the other communities in the war. Perhaps a couple of thousand. The numbers ethnically cleansed or fleeing in front of Muslim advances was -- was much higher, certainly in the tens of thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not waste time about the figures. There are figures available about this, and there will be occasion to ascertain them. When making your statement, as I can see, you spoke to the investigators, Todd Cleaver and Stephen Upton, and as far as I can see from paragraph 15 of your statement -- let me just find it for a moment. Actually, that is the first paragraph of your chronology, the beginning of your chronology. So tell me, please, within the framework of that chronology, are you providing your comments to documents presented to you by these gentlemen that you were interviewed by?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So these are your comments on documents presented to you by them. Is it true that this chronology is not exhaustive and that it doesn't cover all events?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harland, is it true that particularly lacking are reports on incidents provoked by the Muslim side, that is Muslim violations of cease-fires agreed on the Sarajevo battlefront, as well as reports on crimes committed by the Muslim side against the Serb civilians and the army of Republika Srpska? Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. On the contrary, in fact. We had -- we suffered, as perhaps all onlookers suffer, from only being able to report what you saw, and we were overwhelmingly able to see what happened on Muslim-controlled territory. So in fact, when -- when there was a violation of the cease-fire by the Muslims, we were much more likely to see it than when there was a violation of the cease-fire by the Serbs. And similarly, when there was a human rights abuse by the Muslims, we would often see it very directly. We all lived in Sarajevo, which is a rather small geographical area. There were many thousands of us on Muslim-controlled territory. There were very, very few of us on Serb-controlled territory. So in general, we were only able to record the abuses on Serb-held territory when we encountered people who were ethnically cleansed from Serb-held territory who were arriving in the Muslim-controlled areas where we were stationed. In fact, it was a particular source of grievance with the Muslim authorities, that they felt that we were constantly holding them to a higher standard in terms of abuses of human rights and cease-fire violations than that to which we were holding the Serbs. In fact, I think we were not prejudiced against the Muslims, but it probably is true that we saw more of their wrongdoing, of their misdeeds, both in terms of cease-fires and in terms of human rights than we saw of the Serbs. So our reporting measured against an objective recording of the events somewhat later would probably show more attention focused on Muslim cease-fire violations and other actions than would be statistically merited. And we did undertake a little study of this -- of this nature which broadly confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm going to interrupt now. It's time -- past the time for the break. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, could you please continue giving me as concise answers as possible, because I don't have too much time. From what you're saying, it follows that in view of the fact that you were in the centre of town held by the Muslim forces that you were able to note every cease-fire violation by the Muslim side. Does that mean that you did actually report on each of those violations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: My particular role was political reporting, but yes, UNPROFOR certainly had a deployment of UNMOs, military observers, whose principal job was to count the shells and to note what type they were and where they were coming from and going to, and, yes, that was part of UNPROFOR's daily work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 16, you mention the weekly political assessment for Bosnia-Herzegovina number 24, dated the 16th of July, referring to a meeting of the newly-appointed commander, General Briquemont, Viktor Andreev, and yourself with Radovan Karadzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in the report you mention that, "Karadzic noted that even though Republika Srpska had supported exchanges of population, the Serbs recognise the right of people of different ethnic origin to remain or return to their homes if they so wish." Was that his position, the one that he advocated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also say that you raised the issue of ethnic cleansing, particularly in Bijeljina, and that Radovan Karadzic would seek justification for ethnic cleansing. Is that your comment? He would seek to justify it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you talk about Bijeljina, are you familiar with Radovan Karadzic's order dated the 1st of January, 1994, relating precisely to Bijeljina? And since I have it here in the Serbian language, signed and with a stamp, the 1st January 1994 number 01-0894, and it says, "To the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska and President of the Supreme Military Court. According to information about the work of the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina --" I am mentioning this order because it refers to Bijeljina that you referred to -- "indicates many missions being made, particularly the release of persons who are suspected of serious crimes. Such an attitude has worsened the security and political situation in Brcko and Bijeljina. The situation requires that the military prosecutor office's work be examined and any errors and omissions be established made by the prosecutor. It is your duty to act according to this order and to report me about your findings." This was written by Dr. Radovan Karadzic and signed by him. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence, please, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us see the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what I have read out, and I read it accurately, I hope that is not at issue, it should be beyond doubt that Radovan Karadzic advocated the more efficient work of the military prosecutor's office in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll mark this for identification next Defence number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The document will get the next number. The map, which I see the registrar still has, can be returned to the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document is Defence Exhibit 212, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he's advocating that persons who have committed criminal offences should not be released from detention, and he says that this worsens the general security situation in Bijeljina. And he's instructing urgent intervention and inspection of the work of the military prosecutor's office specifically in Bijeljina. Do you know what the status of Muslims was in the area of Bijeljina at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the -- during the war, there were some Muslim communities, some Muslims in the town of Bijeljina and some small Muslim communities around Bijeljina which had remained there until -- at least until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So they remained there under normal living conditions. They were treated in a non-discriminatory fashion. Is that -- does that correspond to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They -- first of all, there were -- there was a constant stream of people from Bijeljina and the Bijeljina area who were being ethnically cleansed. There were some communities -- I remember in particular representatives of one village came to us and said that they were obliged to pay large amounts of money, or at least large by their standards, as a sort of protection racket. If they paid off the local authorities, military and civilian, then they could expect some degree of protection. So there was a residual Muslim minority there, which made it different from other places, you know, such as Visegrad or Rogatica, other places in Eastern Bosnia. But it would be wrong to describe their lives as normal. I should also -- I know you want me to be brief and that's right, but we had a particular problem with Dr. Karadzic's utterances, both in writing and spoken, that there was, in general, a very large variance between what he would say to us and even what he would write and say that he had issued as orders and what actually happened. He would constantly, when we complained about, for example, a cease-fire violation, say, "It's okay. I have given written orders." And he would sometimes even show us the written orders. And then we would see one of the military commanders affected by those orders, and they would say, "Oh, no, we didn't really get them," or, "They certainly weren't carried out and it wasn't Karadzic's real intention that they were carried out." So I would view with some caution his written order, and I wouldn't take it as evidence that whatever he suggested in that letter actually happened. I don't know this particular case and I don't know what the military court was doing, but I would be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, if you could tell us who specifically he was who said that -- who didn't get the order from Karadzic or they didn't carry out what was ordered by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, I should say that there are a lot of such cases, but one which stays in my mind is during the siege of Gorazde in the spring of 1994 - I suppose it's April 1994 - when we were with Dr. Karadzic in Pale while Serb forces in the field were operating a few dozen kilometres to the east of us. And Dr. Karadzic assured us that he had ordered a halt to the advance of Serb forces and that he had ordered a cease-fire. And when it was reported to General Rose, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. remember, at one of these meetings in Pale by his people on the ground that the Serbs were in fact continuing to fire, Dr. Karadzic went and said he was sending -- he repeated the order, and he was sending also a written order. Then later, at the next meeting, we saw General Mladic, and we had already seen him on television in Gorazde, and when we asked him about that, even in the presence of Dr. Karadzic, he laughed about it and said that he was -- he had not received orders that he should not continue to prosecute his attack and that he should do so. And then Dr. Karadzic didn't even say that he hadn't lied, he just came up with a different story. He said, "Well, actually, Lord Owen promised us up to the river in Gorazde." Another fact which he just made up. "And so all we're doing is taking that part of Gorazde which is rightfully ours." And it was so appalling all this business with Karadzic making up facts as convenient, that I was with -- at this time with Vitaly Churkin, who was a representative of the Russian Federation, and he came outside and said, "I give up. I can't negotiate with him any more. I've never heard more lies than I have heard here in the last 48 hours." I could give many such examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 18, you refer to a meeting held on the 5th of August at Pale with Briquemont, Hayes and Andreev, and that meeting was held at Karadzic's initiative. Isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As this doesn't correspond to your statement that he keeps doing something other than he says, is it true that Karadzic made proposals for the withdrawal of forces of the army of Republika Srpska from Mount Igman and establishing secure routes in and out of Sarajevo and cooperation for the restoration of public utilities? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did that indeed happen? Is it true that the army of Republika Srpska withdrew from Igman, et cetera, in accordance with this agreement? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He wasn't forced to withdraw, but he did withdraw in agreement with you, that is your commanders, and this area was taken over by the UNPROFOR forces. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 14th of August, 1993, upon Karadzic's initiative that I now mentioned, a safe area was established in the territory of Igman and Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a demilitarised zone, not a safe area, yes. I don't believe it was the initiative of Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Demilitarised. It was his initiative, a demilitarised zone. Was a component part of that agreement that the Serbs withdraw from 13 checkpoints which were to have been taken over by UNPROFOR and that the Muslim forces could not take over that area? Wasn't that the agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, is it true that the Muslims only a month later, without being prevented by UNPROFOR at all, did capture those points though they had been ceded to UNPROFOR? And on that occasion, that is during this offensive and the takeover of points, they killed 37 and wounded 34 soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska? Surely you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact numbers, but it is true that Muslim forces were consistently and over a long period of time and on a substantial scale in violation of the Mount Igman agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in this chronology which you have produced, is there any reference to this event and the cheating by the Muslim side and the passiveness of the UNPROFOR command which did not react to that at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, yes, there are references, principally in the section on 1994, as you will see. I must also object to the idea that UNPROFOR was passive. In fact, you have -- you've illuminated an important point, which is that in general, the Muslims did not want the status quo. They did not want a cease-fire with the lines that existed in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. They opposed a general cease-fire, and when they made a cease-fire, they did often break that cease-fire. And the commander of UNPROFOR forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, General Rose, did argue very vigorously with the Bosnian Muslim leadership, particularly with Dr. Ganic, who he felt was the principal advocate of this policy of violating cease-fire agreements, and he -- he even sought to threaten them with the use of air attacks by NATO forces on occasions if they would not comply. No such airstrikes ever took place and would not have been agreed to by NATO, it was felt, but UNPROFOR was certainly trying to stabilise the situation, and General Rose was very aware of and very concerned by violations from the Muslim side, particularly with respect to this agreement which we're discussing now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the UNPROFOR command indirectly enable the Muslims to take control of these points which the Serbs had voluntarily abandoned in the interest of bringing the Muslims back to the negotiating table, that is, in the interest of shifting the events from war to peace negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. UNPROFOR certainly didn't enable them to it -- to do it, and in fact, the Muslim forces made considerable efforts to try and avoid detection by us. I recall sitting with the commander of the French battalion which was responsible for that area and going over with him the night vision photographs taken by intelligence officers, showing some degree of infiltration into the zone by -- by Muslim fighters who were trying to -- trying to avoid detection by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you are refuting the statement that you enabled them to do that. But the second part of my question had to do with the reasons for which the Serbs left Igman or ceded Igman. Will you confirm that at least? The aim was to bring the Muslims back to the negotiating table, that they should switch from the tracks of war to the tracks of peace negotiations. Is that part correct at least?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the point. In paragraph 22 you referred to the 15th of October and a meeting between Andreev, Briquemont, De Mello, with Karadzic and Krajisnik at Pale. Is it true that at that meeting Karadzic said that he had issued orders to shop the shelling and sniping, but at the same time, he said that artillery and sniper fire from the Muslim side was a major problem? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you have any knowledge that Karadzic did indeed order units of the army of Republika Srpska to stop shelling or sniping or at least to use it only proportionately?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see here in paragraph 22 that General Briquemont said that he had seen no evidence of Muslim preparations for an attack on the Serb areas but that the Serb shelling of civilian areas was increasing. And in general, I would say that one of the complications of UNPROFOR's work was that the -- the Muslim authorities did have -- see themselves as having an interest in breaking the cease-fires, if necessary, in order not to allow the confrontation lines to stabilise when they, who were about half of the population of Bosnia, were then only living on 18 per cent of the territory. So they -- that created a problem for us. And a sort of opposite problem for us was that the Serbs had an interest in keeping as much military pressure on the Muslims as possible without actually attracting any negative attention. So in a way, both sides were deceiving us though for rather different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But if the Serbs favoured a cease-fire, the cease-fire, and I think you'll agree, Mr. Harland, isn't a political solution. A cease-fire enables the sides to seek a settlement through negotiation and not through loss of life. I assume that is what you advocated for, to have the peace fire -- cease-fire observed.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. And the problem we had with the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was that they felt that if there was a general cease-fire in which the population under their control, about half of the total population of 4 million of the country, if that -- if they were left on 18 per cent of the territory of the country and the cease-fire stabilised but there was no successful outcome to the talks, then they would be left in a very difficult position. So we felt that they were publicly saying that they wanted a cease-fire because it's a hard thing to say you don't want, but in fact were often working to undermine those cease-fires. On the other side, the Serbs genuinely did want the situation to stabilise because they had so much territory, but they also wanted to make life as miserable as possible, through shelling and sniping, of the Serb positions -- of Muslim positions, and Dr. Karadzic even told us that directly, that the sniping and the cutting off of the water serves a purpose. So UNPROFOR was in a particularly difficult position between those two parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I ask you whether you know if Karadzic ordered the units of the army of Republika Srpska to reduce or stop their operations, I have in mind a document to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the commanders of the brigades. That's who it is addressed to, of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, which means from the Main Staff down to the corps command and the brigade commands. The date is the 7th of February, 1994, where it states: "There is proof and evidence that on Muslim artillery provocations, the Serb side is responding inadequately, sometimes even 20 to 30 and even 70 times more. The international community does not criticise us for responding, but that too much force is being used, and the Muslims are provoking us to use our ammunition without effect. The Muslim side is very skillful in ascribing its artillery shelling in town to us, which causes great damage to us and threatens us the loss of our state." And then it says: "I order strict control in responding to provocations and to respond only when we are under threat ourselves and when there is full military justification for doing so. Respond by targeting only military facilities and respond exclusively pursuant to the commander's orders, and respond in the ratio of one to one with the strength of the provocation used." And then it says in figures, "1-1." "Second, exclude any shelling out of control. Control conduct and sanction misdemeanors urgently and on the basis of the law. For corps artilleries, the corps commander shall be responsible to me directly, and the brigade commander for the brigades. Please inform me immediately of any incidents. The Supreme Commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic." And the signature is his, the stamp says Republika Srpska, the header is Republika Srpska, the president of the Republic in Sarajevo, and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. May, I'd like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, the witness can answer or give a comment about it. Have you ever heard of this document, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of this document, but -- and I should say Mr. Milosevic has jumped forward a few months in time. We're now at the beginning of 1994, after the Markale shelling. And I should say that the document is almost certainly a true copy, because at that time, the Serbs were very concerned that as a result of the marketplace massacre, NATO might intervene against them, and they did call us to say that they had passed orders of this type. So I think it is almost certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, if it could be handed in. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D213, MFI, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a comment on this. It is precisely Karadzic which is indicating this response which isn't in kind and to the same ratio, and he draws the attention of the parties that it should be on a one-to-one ratio and that he is seeking strict control in responding to the provocations, strict supervision of that response. Isn't that right? Now, Mr. Harland, does this coincide and compare with what Karadzic said at the 15th of October meeting, 1993? May we hear your comments on that, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commitments that the Serbs gave us to a cease-fire in October of 1993 were not observed. They continued their military activity. And we kept a daily record, as I said before, of the shooting which largely confirmed this. They may have passed the order, but the order was not significantly obeyed if it was passed at all. The situation which you have just referred to, however, was very different. By February of 1994, the Serbs did seem genuinely to want a stabilisation of the situation around Sarajevo, and they did stop shooting. And in fact, they did so -- they reduced the amount of fire coming from their side of the confrontation line from February of 1994 right through till the autumn of 1994 to a very low level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Practically from the beginning of 1994, in fact, until the end of the autumn of 1994; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, beginning almost immediately after the so-called Markale incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to the Markale incident. But in paragraph 26, you say that in your weekly political assessment of the 3rd of November of 1993, mention that in the forward command post, forward headquarters, there were two Muslim snipers who were active and who even shot at UN staff members and the passersby, and that the 1st Corps, the one holding Sarajevo, claimed that it was individuals that had -- belonging to a man called Caco, this gang of individuals under the command of Caco; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I assist you? It is tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just to compare facts, Mr. Harland, this man Caco, was that a nickname for Musan Topalovic who had under his control the left bank of the Miljacka river on the territory of Stari Grad municipality in Sarajevo? Was that who he was?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, though he was dead by the time of this claim, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this man Caco, for which the ABiH 1st Command claimed was a renegade, that he was a commander of a Mountain Brigade of the BH army and so at no event could he have been a renegade, in actual fact? Is that correct, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe what it -- what it says is that is that the snipers who were acting at this time were -- they reported to us that these were renegade supports of Caco. In other words, the period which is being reported here is the period immediately or some weeks after the death of Caco. Caco was killed by Muslim forces in Sarajevo. And when we were complaining about the activity of Muslim snipers in Sarajevo who appeared to be firing at targets within Sarajevo itself, other Muslims, they -- BH 1st Corps, they recognised that these incidents had happened, but they said that this was not part of their policy, this was the act of these so-called renegade supporters of Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, supporters of Caco, who was commander of the Mountain Brigade the BH army. So he couldn't have about a renegade at all. And now, do you know that these formations perpetrated mass killings of Serbs in Bisipoto [phoen], Popodija and Kazani on the slopes of Mount Trbevic in Sarajevo? Do you have an awareness of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we made some efforts to establish the events surrounding those -- those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you establish it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There certainly had been Serbs from Sarajevo killed and their bodies put in the pits of -- of Kazani above Bistrik barracks, and that the people who did it were certainly associated with -- with Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in a television programme --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- Alija Izetbegovic referred to Caco as his son? He called him "My son."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, wasn't it Karadzic at a meeting of the 15th of October who indicated the danger from Muslim sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that General Rose, at a meeting with Ganic, for the umpteenth time indicated the mortar fire that was coming from the Muslim side from a mortar installed on trucks, mortars on trucks, and sniper fire opened by the Muslims at their own people? Isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Rose did make that protest, and it was our concern that certainly some elements and probably including the leadership of the Bosnian Muslims did not wish to stabilise the situation around Sarajevo, and that was very frustrating for General Rose. Can I just add, though, that concerning the killings of the people at Kazani and Caco's actions, Caco was the commander of -- of a brigade and was very ruthless in the way he dealt with Muslims. He was certainly also a murderer in the way he dealt with Serbs. My sense, however -- I met him, and I met the authorities who dealt with him. My sense was that whatever President Izetbegovic may have said, the Muslim leadership generally considered him dangerous, and ultimately they did kill him on, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think, towards the end of October 1993. So I would not make a line of questioning that suggests that there was a general policy to kill Serbs in Sarajevo. And although the numbers, perhaps several dozen, were shocking, it was really in no way comparable to the crimes that were being committed by the Serbs. And I don't know if it was the intention to make an equation, but that would be a wrong conclusion to draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't the general option. How come so many Serbs were killed in Sarajevo then?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most Serbs who -- most of the Serbs who were killed within the confrontation lines of Sarajevo were killed by Serb fire coming from outside the confrontation line, either by snipers or by shelling. We kept a rough tally of the number of people killed in Sarajevo by visits to the morgue, by taking reports from family and by our own observations, and our impressions were that although the crimes of Caco were very horrible, they were relatively limited in scope and that most of the Serb casualties in Sarajevo were not caused by actions from the -- from the Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Harland. The killing of Serbs in Sarajevo, do you exclusively link that up to this group of men around Caco or do you allow for the possibility that that was done by many more groups, units, members of the army, the so-called army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not exclusively done by Caco, though I would -- from the figures that came to us, I would guess that perhaps most of the Serbs killed in Sarajevo by Muslim groups were killed by groups associated with Caco. But there were certainly -- you're correct. There were certainly other Serb victims too, though I hope during this whole line of questioning we are again clear that there is no equation in numbers or even in order of magnitude between what was happening in Sarajevo and what was happening in Serb-controlled territory around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why it can't be compared. Perhaps there were a thousand of you there in Sarajevo. But we don't have time for that. Anyway, in your weekly political assessment of the 9th of February, in paragraph 26, you speak about the tragedy that took place at the Markale marketplace, the 5th of February, 1994; is that right? That report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, through force of circumstance that your testimony was interrupted, in fact, and in my material, the documents that I received, along with Lord Owen's testimony, who completed his testimony here yesterday, in those CD-ROM materials there is part of a BBC programme which was attached to Lord Owen's book, and the title is "Jankovi the 30th of October, 1995, BBC Panorama, Peace Without Honour, The Propaganda War," and it quoted a UN document. So I'm asking you here and now whether you remember that. It was quoted in the document that I was disclosed: "Most immediate code restricted 8th of February, 1994 [In English] From UN Command Sarajevo to UN New York. Judging from the trajectory, experts thought -- experts thought that range is more likely -- that the range is more likely to be under 2.000 metres than 2 to 4.000 metres, putting it in Muslim territory rather than Serb." [Interpretation] Tell me now, please, in view of the position you held and this report which I assume you know about, would it be true that there was a lot of information pointing to the fact that that was fired from the Muslim side, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with that document, but I am not familiar with the BBC broadcast you refer to. With respect to the first Markale massacre, and I should say that there is controversy surrounding who fired the shell in both the first Markale massacre and the second Markale massacre, but in respect of the first one, which we are discussing now, the UNPROFOR conclusion was that it could not be determined beyond reasonable doubt who had fired the first -- the shell for the first Markale massacre. The report that you have just quoted was a very preliminary report which is, in the normal course of events, followed up by a full ballistic analysis. Now, the more comprehensive report, which followed a couple of days after the one which you have in your hand, concluded in fact that the range from which the mortar was fired, the possible ranges from which the mortar is fired crossed the confrontation line to the north-east of the Markale marketplace. In other words, it was fired from close to the confrontation line, but it was not possible for us to determine whether it was fired from the Muslim side or the Serb side. And in fact, there is -- there is a factual error in the calculations made for the first report which was noted in the fuller report that followed a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the finale of it was, the conclusion was that nothing can be said with absolute certainty. The first indications showed that it was from the Muslim side, and then the finale of it was that one couldn't make an absolutely correct assertion. Isn't that right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I should say that that was often the case. For any given shell, it was very difficult for us to say where it came from. Only some shells could it be confirmed with great accuracy where they came from. When we were able to determine, then in almost a hundred per cent of cases we were able to determine that shells landing on the Muslim side of the confrontation line came from the Serb side of the confrontation line. We had mortar detecting radars, which the Serbs tried to destroy. We had military observers who --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I'm just asking you about this specific instance. So you needn't tell me that there were shells fired from the Serb side. What we're talking about is the Markale marketplace. The first report was that it came from the Muslim side; the final conclusion that nothing definite could be established; and third, that there was a general anti-Serb hysteria that it was the Serbs who actually perpetrated this crime. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I must say I have sometimes accused General Rose of things, but I've never accused him of anti-Serb hysteria. On the contrary. I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that there was -- there was, in a way, in fact, in certain parts of UNPROFOR a certain sympathy with the Serb military, because I think because the Serb military more closely represented a military like that from which they came. So it was certainly not my experience with UNPROFOR that the reporting of UNPROFOR reflected any anti-Serb hysteria. On the contrary; my experience with that reporting was that it went out of the way to give the benefit of the doubt to the Serb side. And in this case, it was determined by engineers who, as far as I remember, had no obvious political views at all, that it could not be determined who fired that shell, and that remains the UNPROFOR position, though I feel it is also fair to put in the context that that was often true, we could not confirm, and in almost a hundred per cent of the cases where we could confirm where a shell came from, landing on the Muslim side, it came from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you have made an inversion of theses. I never intimated that General Rose launched an anti-Serb hysteria. I wasn't watching, maybe the translation wasn't quite accurate. On the one hand you had reports that it had come from the Muslim side and then the final conclusion that it was not possible to determine where it had come from. Whereas on the other hand there was a worldwide media propaganda along anti-Serb lines that the crime had been committed by the Serbs. I'm not saying that the source was General Rose. On the contrary; I think that he was quite objective.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lost translation. First it got very small and then I lost translation. Okay. Let me try. First of all, I -- I don't believe that the reporting from UNPROFOR was anything other than objective. And from your own reporting, from your own comment from the BBC, they are willing to present a preliminary report which is really very favourable to the Serb view of that event, but they do not, at least as you've described the show, appear to discuss the conclusive report. So I don't think that this media hysteria went as far as the BBC. In fact, I remember quite by coincidence several years later listening to a BBC correspondent, Nick Gowing, who is still a correspondent, a presenter, talking about that incident and saying how it was actually the Muslims who had done that. In fact, he was thereby perpetrating as a fact something which really wasn't known by any of the people who had investigated the incident on the ground. We could -- we wished as much as everybody else that there was a clear answer to the question, but the fact was there was no clear answer to the question. It is still not able to be determined on the basis of the ballistic evidence who fired that shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, well, that is the whole point. I'm not saying that you were a source of information, and especially not General Rose. But what I am saying are -- I'm referring to certain coincidences. On the one hand, you were not a source of the information that the Serbs had fired the shell, whereas there was an anti-Serb media hysteria that the crime had been committed by the Serbs. And this programme, which is on a CD together with Lord Owen's book, was broadcast on the 30th of October, 1995, so it's much later. And I read out to you from that programme a document that you said you were familiar with and which says that the range was within 2.000 metres and not between 2 and 4.000 metres, which seems to point to the Muslim side. But before that telegram of the 8th of February that I quoted from, there's another telegram that is quoted dated the 6th of February, and it is quoted in the same documents that were attached to Lord Owen's testimony. It is also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't know if the witness can follow all this detail. I really don't think we're going to get much further with this. The witness has given you what sounds to be an objective account, that nobody is certain, he says, as they understood it, where the shell came from. Now, going over and over this again with a witness who can't himself say, of course, where the shell came from seems to me -- just a moment -- seems to me to be a waste of time, and we need to move on to some other point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am moving on to something else, namely the witness said that he was familiar with this dispatch that I quoted from, and now I am asking him about another dispatch that doesn't relate to Markale but was sent on the same time -- at the same time from Zagreb to New York, on the 6th of February, and it refers to a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says: "Care is particularly important -- [In English] Care is particularly important given the fact that UNPROFOR is almost hundred per cent sure that the Bosniaks on at least two occasions during the past 18 months have been the origin of shelling that caused casualties in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Are you familiar with that report? You probably remember it too.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was sent from Zagreb, but I am familiar with the assertion and the evidence on which it's based, which came from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you familiar that the assertion regarding the massacre in the bread line in Vase Miskina Street on the 27th of May, 1992, that that too was provoked by the Muslims, and for propaganda purposes, and it was successful, because three days later the Security Council adopted Resolution 757 enforcing sanctions against Serbia. Are you aware of that, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Let the witness answer these questions. If it's 1992, it sounds as though it may have been before your time, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was before my time. I'm familiar with the place and with the incident and with the claim by both sides that the other side fired it. But Mr. Milosevic has raised the -- the question of who fired which shell, so if I can just add, to clarify, that about a half a million shells were fired at Sarajevo during the course of the war. Sometimes we were able to determine very exactly where they came from and sometimes we weren't. In nearly a hundred per cent of the cases, that is with the exception of two or three, when we could confirm, we confirmed that they came from the Serb side. And I think that all of our discussion is basically going around that point. Are there some particular shells which are in the grey zone? Yes. Is this one of them? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, Mr. Harland, Mr. Harland, regarding this bread line about which there is evidence that the shot was fired by the Muslims, and relating to Markale for which there is evidence that the Muslim side fired it, this provoked the worst possible consequences for the Serb side. So it is very difficult --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been over this point. It's pointless going on. Let's move on to something else. The time is limited. Your time is limited, and the Court's time is limited, and to go over the same argument trying to make the same points and trying to argue the witness into some position or other is a waste of time. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
